title: Landscape
medium: Handscroll in six sections; ink and color on paper

altText: A section of a handscroll showing a mountain landscape painted in ink and soft color on paper, with rocky peaks and scenery arranged across a wide horizontal view.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, artist, date, medium (handscroll in six sections), period (Qing dynasty), tags (Mountains, Landscapes), public-domain flag, credit line and image URLs read from the record. The record gives no further description of the scenery.

context: A handscroll in six sections, dated 1898, by Song Nian, painted in ink and color on paper in the late Qing dynasty. The record lists mountains and landscape as its subject. It was made only a little more than a decade before the end of imperial rule in China in 1912.

descriptions.k: This long painting shows mountains. It is painted with ink and soft color. It is made in six parts that you look at one by one. Which mountain do you like most? Where would you walk first?
descriptions.g12: Song Nian painted this mountain scroll in 1898 in China. It has six sections, like six chapters of a story. He used ink and soft color on paper. As you look from one end to the other, the view changes. Which section would you want to visit?
descriptions.g35: Song Nian dated this landscape 1898, near the end of the Qing dynasty, the last imperial dynasty of China. It is a handscroll in six sections, painted with ink and color on paper. As the scroll unrolls, the mountains and scenery change from place to place. How might a painter connect six sections so that they feel like one journey?
descriptions.g68: Painted in 1898, this handscroll belongs to the last years of the Qing dynasty, when landscape painting still drew on centuries of tradition. The record describes it as having six sections, which suggests a landscape designed to unfold over time. Ink and color on paper build mountains and scenery. How do changes from section to section keep a long landscape from feeling repetitive?
descriptions.g910: Dated 1898, Song Nian's handscroll is a late Qing landscape in the long tradition of mountains and waters painting. The six sections are experienced sequentially, so composition becomes a matter of pacing, transitions, and variation of density. Ink and color on paper allow both structure and atmosphere. Consider how the artist might balance tradition and personal choice at a time when imperial China was nearing the end of its long history.
descriptions.g1112: A late Qing handscroll like this one raises questions about how artists inherited a deep landscape tradition during a period of rapid historical change. The scroll, dated 1898, is recorded in six sections, which stresses sequential viewing and the idea of landscape as journey. Because the record offers little description, readings must come from visual evidence in each section. How does a long format shape meaning, and what is the relationship between tradition and its moment?

teacherNote.context: Dated 1898, this handscroll in six sections is by Song Nian, in the final years of the Qing dynasty. The record gives no scene description, so base discussion on what students see.
directions: Have students plan a six-part scroll as a storyboard of a journey, with one sketch per section.
Discuss how an artist can honor a tradition and still make something personal.
Compare this scroll's mood with the Ming handscroll from another day in the series.
